Method: cloud.google.com/compute/vm-instance-pricing is now only an index page, and the pricing pages are too large for the fetch tool, so the per-family pages (cloud.google.com/products/compute/pricing/general-purpose, /compute-optimized, /storage-optimized) and cloud.google.com/spot-vms/pricing were downloaded and their embedded 'Iowa (us-central1)' hourly tables parsed. Per-vCPU, per-GB and per-GiB-SSD component rates came from Google's SKU catalog (cloud.google.com/skus), read in a browser. Every whole-machine price computed from the SKU rates matches Google's listed machine price to at least 6 decimals, except the two C3D -lssd shapes, which Google does not list.

c3d-standard-180-lssd and c3d-standard-360-lssd: the all-in totals are DERIVED (Google-listed base machine price + generic Local SSD rate of $0.08/GiB-month on-demand, $0.0478 Spot). The inference that the generic Local SSD SKU applies rests on (a) no C3D Local SSD SKU existing in the catalog and (b) docs classing C3D storage as original Local SSD, not Titanium SSD. The on-demand total agrees with the third-party gcloud-compute.com figure ($17.6587 for the 360 shape); its Spot figure ($4.722) is about 4% above the $4.523 computed here.

Spot prices are variable. Google's Spot pricing page and Spot docs say they can change up to once every day (the disk pricing page still carries older wording of 'once every 30 days'). Treat every Spot figure as a 2026-11-20 snapshot. Spot VMs can be preempted at any time and Spot capacity for very large shapes (192-384 vCPU, whole-host H4D) is not guaranteed; availability was not and could not be checked here.

H4D Spot: prices and Spot SKUs are published for us-central1, and the Spot docs do not exclude H4D, but the H4D docs section itself only says 'available on-demand, or with one- and three-year CUDs'. Confirm Spot H4D can actually be created before relying on the Spot figure.

C4D memory is priced per gigabyte (10^9 bytes) while machine memory is in GiB; the per-GB SKU must be multiplied by 1.073741824. Using the raw SKU rate against the GiB figure under-prices C4D by about 2%. All other families here are priced per GiB.

Local SSD per-GiB-month SKUs are converted to hourly by Google at 730 hours per month (confirmed by matching listed machine prices). For H4D, C4D and Z4D the Titanium SSD is a separate billing SKU yet already included in the listed -lssd machine price; ondemand_usd_hour and spot_usd_hour for all -lssd shapes in this output are all-in, and local_ssd_usd_hour is the on-demand SSD portion of that total (not an extra).

Not included in any figure: boot or data disks (C4D, H4D and Z4D accept Hyperdisk only), network egress, Tier_1 networking, snapshots, tax. H4D internet-bound bandwidth is limited to 1 Gbps and H4D has no live migration, which may matter for a build that pulls large sources.

Physical cores: only H4D gives one full core per vCPU (192 cores). On C4D, C3D, Z4D, N2D and C2D a vCPU is one SMT thread, so core counts are half the vCPU counts. Per physical core-hour, H4D is by far the cheapest on-demand (about $0.041 vs $0.085-$0.12 for the others); on Spot, H4D (about $0.020) and C3D (about $0.021-$0.025) are closest.
Sustained use discounts: only N2D is eligible (max 20%), and only beyond 25% of a billing month, never on Spot, so it is irrelevant to a one-off build.

Third-party cross-checks (NOT first-party, context only): gcloud-compute.com c3d-standard-360-lssd as above; an aggregator search snippet showed c4d-standard-384 at $18.1431 on-demand (agrees with Google's $18.143126) and $8.0368 Spot (Google's page today: $7.635695), consistent with Spot drift.
Quota rules and zone-level availability of these shapes in us-central1 were not part of this step and were not researched.

Spot prices are not fixed: Google's Spot page says they 'can change up to once every day' (another Google page says up to once every 30 days). The Spot figures are today's snapshot and should be re-read just before the build. Spot VMs can be preempted at any time and Local SSD data does not survive preemption.
Memory and disk are priced per GiB (binary). Prices are USD, exclude tax, Linux with no licence fees, no committed-use discounts.

Machine prices exclude boot/data disks, network egress and any premium OS image. C4 cannot use Persistent Disk, so a C4 build needs at least a Hyperdisk Balanced boot disk ($0.000109589/GiB-hour capacity in Iowa, plus IOPS/throughput above the free baseline). N2 and M3 can use Persistent Disk.

For the C4 -lssd shapes the hourly prices given already include the Titanium SSD charge (as Google's own table does); the local_ssd_usd_hour field is the on-demand portion of that total, not an extra.

Billing is per second with a one-minute minimum, so a 1-2 day run costs hours x hourly rate with no rounding to whole days or months. The 24 h / 48 h figures in the arithmetic are my multiplication of Google's hourly prices.

Sustained-use discounts: only N2 is eligible, and a 1-2 day run earns $0 unless the same billing account has other N2 usage in us-central1 that month pushing aggregated usage past 25% of the month. C4 and M3 get none. Spot usage never earns SUDs.

Physical core counts are vCPUs / 2, derived from Google's statement that these series have two vCPUs (hardware threads) per core by default; Google does not publish a per-machine-type core count table.

Availability and quota were not checked (no cloud account access was used). Google's docs say N2 Ice Lake (required for 96+ vCPU N2) and M3 are offered only in specific regions/zones; large shapes normally also need a regional CPU quota increase (per-family quotas for C4 and M3), which is outside this pricing task.

M3 facts on Local SSD count and Spot support came from an automated summary of Google's memory-optimized machines page rather than a direct read of the table; the M3 CPU model and all M3 prices were read directly.

Third-party cross-check (cloudprice.net, data stamped 2026-11-20 03:02 UTC, not a Google source): n2-standard-128 $6.2156/h, c4-highmem-192 $12.5125/h, m3-megamem-128 $14.4096/h on-demand in us-central1 - all agree with Google's figures. It showed no Spot prices. Other aggregators surfaced by search disagreed with each other on Spot (e.g. n2-standard-4 at $0.1107 vs $0.0660) and were not used.

storage.option: Local SSD, separately attached 375 GiB partitions (non-Titanium; N2 / N2D / N1 / C2 / C2D)
storage.price_basis: On demand $0.000109589 per GiB-hour in Iowa (us-central1) = $0.08 per GiB-month at Google's 730-hour month. Billed per second on provisioned capacity 'for the lifetime of the VM that it is attached to'; no IOPS or throughput charge. Spot rate $0.000065479 per GiB-hour (variable). Arithmetic: valid disk counts on N2/N2D are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 or 24 (larger machine sizes force a minimum of 4, 8 or 16), so the smallest count that reaches 2 TB is 8 x 375 = 3,000 GiB: 3,000 x 0.000109589 = $0.328767/hr x 24 = $7.89/day. For reference 6 x 375 = 2,250 GiB would be $0.246575/hr = $5.92/day, but 6 is a valid count only on N1. Spot: 3,000 x 0.000065479 = $0.196437/hr = $4.71/day.
storage.performance: NVMe, 4 to 8 disks (1,500 to 3,000 GiB): 680,000 read / 360,000 write IOPS and 2,650 / 1,400 MiB/s read / write; N2 and N2D need at least 24 vCPUs (N1: 32) to reach this. One disk: 170,000 / 90,000 IOPS, 660 / 350 MiB/s. SCSI is lower (8 disks: 400,000 / 280,000 IOPS, 1,560 / 1,090 MiB/s). Far above the stated 150 MB/s write need.
storage.survives_stop: No by default. Stop, suspend, guest-OS shutdown, Spot preemption, an instance max-run-duration STOP, and disabling billing all discard the data; a restarted VM gets blank disks. Data does survive a guest reboot and live migration. A Preview-only option (gcloud beta compute instances stop --discard-local-ssd=false, or REST; not available in the console; max 48 disks) copies the data to durable storage, which is billed as storage and consumes Persistent disk standard GB quota. Cannot be snapshotted or imaged.
storage.compatible_families: Choose-your-own disk count: N1, N2, N2D, C2, C2D (also A2, G2, M1, M3). Disks can only be added at VM creation. C3 and C3D get non-Titanium Local SSD only via fixed-count '-lssd' machine types (c3-standard-44-lssd = 8 disks, c3d-*-90-lssd = 8 disks); I could not find c3/c3d '-lssd' price rows in the page HTML, so their rate is unconfirmed. Not supported: E2, N4, N4A, N4D, H3, T2D, shared-core.

Derived by subtracting the non-lssd price: (c4d-standard-64-lssd $3.517005063 - c4d-standard-64 $3.023854378) / 2,250 GiB = $0.000219178 per GiB-hour = $0.16 per GiB-month, i.e. double the generic Local SSD rate (same result from the 16, 48 and 96 vCPU pairs). C4D component rates, also derived from Google's table (standard-8 vs highmem-8, checked against highcpu-8): $0.0327035 per vCPU-hour and $0.00375335 per GiB-memory-hour. Smallest C4D shape with >= 2 TB is c4d-standard-64-lssd (6 x 375 = 2,250 GiB): 64 x 0.0327035 = 2.093024 + 248 x 0.00375335 = 0.930830 + 2,250 x 0.000219178 = 0.493151 -> $3.517005/hr (matches published) = $84.41/day whole machine, of which the SSD is $0.493151/hr = $11.84/day. c4d-standard-96-lssd (3,000 GiB): 3.139536 + 1.396246 + 0.657534 = $5.193316/hr = $124.64/day (SSD part $15.78/day). c4d-highmem-64-lssd (504 GiB RAM, 2,250 GiB): $4.477862/hr = $107.47/day. c4d-*-48-lssd has only 1,500 GiB. Spot (variable): C4D local SSD $0.000092329 per GiB-hour is published explicitly; c4d-standard-64-lssd Spot $1.480356/hr = $35.53/day.
storage.survives_stop: No. Data is discarded on stop and the Preview 'preserve Local SSD data' option is explicitly not available for machine types that use Titanium SSD. c4d-*-lssd VMs do live migrate through host maintenance. Google also warns that Local SSD on C4, C4A, C4D, C4N and H4D 'might not recover all writes that completed before a power loss event'.
storage.compatible_families: C4D only, in fixed sizes tied to vCPU count: 8/16 vCPU = 375 GiB, 32 = 750, 48 = 1,500, 64 = 2,250, 96 = 3,000, 192 = 6,000, 384 = 12,000 GiB. C4D 'supports only Hyperdisk volumes' and 'doesn't support Persistent Disk', so the boot disk must be Hyperdisk Balanced.

storage.price_basis: Derived from Google's whole-machine tables in the same way. C4: (c4-standard-8-lssd $0.477531781 - c4-standard-8 $0.39534) / 375 GiB = $0.000219178 per GiB-hour = $0.16 per GiB-month; C4 components derived as $0.03465 per vCPU-hour and $0.003938 per GiB-hour. c4-standard-48-lssd (48 vCPU, 180 GiB, 3,000 GiB): 48 x 0.03465 = 1.6632 + 180 x 0.003938 = 0.70884 + 3,000 x 0.000219178 = 0.657534 -> $3.029574/hr = $72.71/day (SSD part $15.78/day). c4-standard-32-lssd (1,875 GiB = 2.01 TB decimal, no headroom): 1.1088 + 0.47256 + 0.410959 = $1.992319/hr = $47.82/day (SSD part $9.86/day). C4A: (c4a-standard-8-lssd $0.482487671 - c4a-standard-8 $0.3592) / 750 GiB = $0.000164384 per GiB-hour = $0.12 per GiB-month; components $0.03086 per vCPU-hour, $0.00351 per GiB-hour; c4a-standard-32-lssd (32 vCPU, 128 GiB, 2,250 GiB) = $1.4368 + 0.369863 = $1.806663/hr = $43.36/day (SSD part $8.88/day). Spot local SSD (published, variable): C4 $0.000131233, C4A $0.000089315 per GiB-hour.
storage.survives_stop: No. Titanium SSD cannot be preserved on stop or suspend; C4A additionally does not support suspend with Titanium SSD attached.
storage.compatible_families: C4 '-lssd' (4 to 288 vCPU; 375 GiB to 18,000 GiB) and C4A '-lssd' (Arm/Axion, 4 to 72 vCPU; 375 to 6,000 GiB). Both families are Hyperdisk-only for persistent storage ('C4 doesn't support Persistent Disk', 'C4A doesn't support Persistent Disk').

storage.option: Z3 storage-optimized machine types (Titanium SSD bundled in 3,000 GiB disks)
storage.price_basis: Whole-machine prices published for Iowa; components not broken out. Derived from three rows: every Z3 shape is 8 GiB per vCPU, and the table fits (vCPU + 8 GiB) = $0.1028955/hr plus SSD at $0.000109589 per GiB-hour ($0.08 per GiB-month); vCPU and memory cannot be separated from this table. z3-highmem-8-highlssd (8 vCPU, 64 GiB, 3,000 GiB): 8 x 0.1028955 = 0.823164 + 3,000 x 0.000109589 = 0.328767 -> $1.151931/hr = $27.65/day. z3-highmem-14-standardlssd (14 vCPU, 112 GiB, 3,000 GiB): 1.440537 + 0.328767 = $1.769304/hr = $42.46/day. z3-highmem-22-standardlssd (22 vCPU, 176 GiB, 6,000 GiB): $2.921235/hr = $70.11/day. SSD portion of 3,000 GiB = $7.89/day. Spot (variable): z3-highmem-8-highlssd $0.637030/hr, z3-highmem-14-standardlssd $0.967474/hr.
storage.performance: One 3,000 GiB disk (z3-highmem-8-highlssd, z3-highmem-14-standardlssd): 750,000 read / 500,000 write IOPS, 3,000 / 2,500 MiB/s. Two disks (6,000 GiB): 1,500,000 / 1,000,000 IOPS, 6,000 / 5,000 MiB/s.
storage.survives_stop: No. Titanium SSD; preserve-on-stop is not available.
storage.compatible_families: Z3 only (8 to 176 vCPU, plus a 192-vCPU bare metal shape); the minimum bundle is 3,000 GiB. Persistent storage on Z3 is Hyperdisk.

storage.price_basis: H4D exists only as 192-vCPU shapes. Iowa: h4d-standard-192 (720 GiB) $7.85376/hr; h4d-highmem-192 (1,488 GiB) $8.842944/hr; h4d-highmem-192-lssd (1,488 GiB + 3,750 GiB Titanium) $9.42409126/hr = $226.18/day. Derived components: memory (8.842944 - 7.85376) / 768 = $0.001288 per GiB-hour; vCPU (7.85376 - 720 x 0.001288) / 192 = $0.036075 per vCPU-hour; SSD (9.42409126 - 8.842944) / 3,750 = $0.000154973 per GiB-hour (about $0.113 per GiB-month) = $0.581147/hr = $13.95/day for the 3,750 GiB bundle.
storage.performance: h4d-highmem-192-lssd: 10 x 375 GiB = 3,750 GiB, 1,500,000 read / 750,000 write IOPS, 6,250 / 3,300 MiB/s. Important: Hyperdisk Balanced on H4D is capped at 15,000 IOPS and 240 MBps per instance, so the local SSD is the only fast storage on this family.
storage.survives_stop: No (Titanium SSD). Live migration is not supported on H4D; maintenance behaviour is terminate/restart with Local SSD data persistence.
storage.compatible_families: H4D only. H4D supports just two block storage types: Hyperdisk Balanced and local Titanium SSD (no Persistent Disk, no Hyperdisk Throughput/Extreme).

storage.option: Hyperdisk Balanced, 2 TiB (2,048 GiB) at 16,000 IOPS and 1,000 MiB/s
storage.price_basis: Iowa: capacity $0.000109589 per GiB-hour ($0.08 per GiB-month); provisioned IOPS $0.000006849 per IOPS-hour ($0.005 per IOPS-month); provisioned throughput $0.000054795 per MiB/s-hour ($0.04 per MiB/s-month). Only performance above the free baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 140 MiB/s is billed. Billed per second on provisioned values until the disk is deleted. Arithmetic: 2,048 x 0.000109589 = $0.224438/hr; (16,000 - 3,000) x 0.000006849 = $0.089037/hr; (1,000 - 140) x 0.000054795 = $0.047124/hr; total $0.360599/hr x 24 = $8.65/day ($5.39 capacity + $2.14 IOPS + $1.13 throughput). At baseline performance only (3,000 IOPS / 140 MiB/s): $5.39/day. At 6,000 IOPS / 300 MiB/s: $6.09/day. Gotcha: if IOPS and throughput are not specified, the defaults for a 2,048 GiB volume are 6 x 2,048 + 3,000 = 15,288 IOPS and MIN(2,400, 1.5 x 2,048 + 140) = 2,400 MiB/s, which bills $10.38/day.
storage.performance: Per volume: 4 GiB to 64 TiB, 3,000 to 160,000 IOPS (volumes >= 320 GiB), 140 to 2,400 MiB/s; throughput must be between MAX(140, IOPS/256) and MIN(2,400, IOPS/4). Also capped by the VM: C4D 16 vCPU 75,000 IOPS / 1,200 MiB/s; C4D 32 and 48 vCPU 75,000 / 1,600; C4D 64 vCPU 160,000 / 2,400; C4D 96 vCPU 160,000 / 3,125; C4 48 vCPU 160,000 / 2,400; N4 32 vCPU 100,000 / 1,600; H4D 15,000 / 240. Limits are shared between reads and writes (half-duplex); IOPS limits assume 4 KB I/O and throughput limits >= 256 KB I/O. Provisioned performance can be changed once every 4 hours; size at most twice per 4 hours. Note the 140 MiB/s baseline is about 147 MB/s, just under the stated 150 MB/s peak write rate.
storage.survives_stop: Yes. Durable network storage; data persists across stop/start and the disk can be detached and re-attached. It keeps billing while the VM is stopped or after the VM is deleted, until the disk itself is deleted.
storage.compatible_families: C3, C3D, C4, C4A, C4D, C4N, N4, N4A, N4D, H3, H4D, Z3, Z4D, M-series, G4 and others. On C2D, E2, N1, N2 and N2D Google says you must contact your account team to use Hyperdisk Balanced. It is the only persistent option on C4, C4A, C4D, N4, N4D and H4D.

storage.option: Hyperdisk Throughput, 2 TiB at its 180 MiB/s maximum (not recommended for this workload)
storage.price_basis: Iowa: capacity $0.000006849 per GiB-hour ($0.005 per GiB-month) plus provisioned throughput $0.000342466 per MiB/s-hour ($0.25 per MiB/s-month); no free baseline. Arithmetic: 2,048 x 0.000006849 = $0.014027/hr + 180 x 0.000342466 = $0.061644/hr = $0.075671/hr = $1.82/day.
storage.performance: HDD-class. Size 2 TiB to 32 TiB; throughput between MAX(20, 5 x TiB) and MIN(90 x TiB, 2,400) MiB/s, so a 2 TiB volume tops out at 180 MiB/s. IOPS cannot be provisioned: 4 IOPS per MiB/s, i.e. only 720 IOPS at 180 MiB/s (9,600 maximum on any volume). Poor fit for 350,000 small files and heavy random memory-mapped reads.
storage.compatible_families: C3, C3D, C4, C4A, C4D, C4N, N2, N2D, N4, N4A, N4D, H3, T2D, G2, Z3 and others. Not H4D.

storage.option: Hyperdisk Extreme, 2 TiB at 16,000 IOPS (overkill; included for completeness)
storage.price_basis: Iowa: capacity $0.000171233 per GiB-hour ($0.125 per GiB-month) plus every provisioned IOPS at $0.000043836 per IOPS-hour ($0.032 per IOPS-month); no free baseline. Arithmetic: 2,048 x 0.000171233 = $0.350685/hr + 16,000 x 0.000043836 = $0.701376/hr = $1.052061/hr = $25.25/day. At the minimum allowed 2 IOPS per GiB (4,096 IOPS): $12.73/day.
storage.performance: 64 GiB to 64 TiB; up to 350,000 IOPS; throughput is not configurable (250 MiB/s per 1,000 IOPS, up to 5,000 MiB/s). Intended for workloads that need more than 160,000 IOPS or 2,400 MiB/s from one volume.
storage.compatible_families: Large shapes only: C4A, C4D, M3, M4 need >= 64 vCPUs; C4 and G4 >= 96; C3 >= 88; C3D >= 60; N2 >= 80. Not H4D, N4 or N4D.

storage.price_basis: Iowa: $0.000136986 per GiB-hour ($0.10 per GiB-month); I/O is included in the capacity price. Billed per second on provisioned size until deleted. Arithmetic: 2,048 x 0.000136986 = $0.280547/hr x 24 = $6.73/day.
storage.performance: Scales with size: baseline 3,000 IOPS + 6 IOPS per GiB and 140 MiB/s + 0.28 MiB/s per GiB, so 2,048 GiB gives up to 15,288 IOPS and about 713 MiB/s; hard caps 80,000 IOPS and 1,200 MiB/s per instance. Also capped by vCPU count, e.g. N2/N2D pd-balanced: 16-31 vCPU 20,000 IOPS, 32-63 vCPU 50,000, 64+ 80,000, with 1,200 MiB/s from 16 vCPU up.
storage.compatible_families: N1, N2, N2D, E2, C3, C3D, C2, C2D, H3 and other older series. NOT available on C4, C4A, C4D, C4N, N4, N4A, N4D or H4D (Google's Persistent Disk support table shows no PD type for those series; the C4, C4A, C4D and N4D pages each say the series doesn't support Persistent Disk).

storage.price_basis: Iowa: $0.000232877 per GiB-hour ($0.17 per GiB-month); I/O included. Arithmetic: 2,048 x 0.000232877 = $0.476932/hr x 24 = $11.45/day.
storage.performance: Baseline 6,000 IOPS + 30 IOPS per GiB and 240 MiB/s + 0.48 MiB/s per GiB, so 2,048 GiB gives up to 67,440 IOPS and hits the 1,200 MiB/s per-instance throughput cap; hard cap 100,000 IOPS. vCPU-tiered, e.g. N2/N2D pd-ssd: 16-31 vCPU 25,000 IOPS, 32-63 vCPU 60,000, 64+ 100,000.
storage.compatible_families: Same as pd-balanced: N1, N2, N2D, E2, C3, C3D, C2, C2D and other older series; not C4, C4A, C4D, N4, N4D or H4D.

storage.billing_rules:
All from Google pages read on 2026-11-20 (first party).

VM granularity and minimum: 'All vCPUs, GPUs, and GB of memory are charged a minimum of 1 minute ... After 1 minute, instances are charged in 1 second increments.' Uptime runs from start until the instance reaches the STOPPING state; an idle VM that is still RUNNING is billed in full. Source: https://cloud.google.com/products/compute/pricing (FAQ; /compute/vm-instance-pricing redirects here).

Disk granularity: 'All disk-related charges in this section are prorated based on a granularity of seconds. This includes all persistent disk types, snapshot storage, and Local SSD pricing.' You pay for provisioned size (and, for Hyperdisk, provisioned IOPS/throughput), used or not, until the disk is deleted. Standard snapshots have a 1-hour minimum. Source: https://cloud.google.com/compute/disks-image-pricing

What a STOPPED (TERMINATED) VM still costs: CPU and memory charges stop (CPU billed only in RUNNING and PENDING_STOP; memory also in SUSPENDING/SUSPENDED). 'For attached resources like disks or external IP addresses, you incur charges while the resources exist, regardless of the compute instance state.' So a stopped VM keeps paying for its boot disk and any Persistent Disk or Hyperdisk at the full rates above (for example a 2 TiB Hyperdisk Balanced keeps costing $5.39 to $8.65 per day), for snapshots, and for a static external IP (a static IP on a stopped VM is charged at the higher unused rate, $0.01/hr versus $0.005/hr in use on a standard VM; an ephemeral IP is released on stop). To stop paying you must delete the disks or the VM. Sources: https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/instance-lifecycle , https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/suspend-stop-reset-instances-overview , https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/stop-start-instance , https://cloud.google.com/vpc/network-pricing

Does a stopped VM with local SSD keep its data: no. 'When you stop or suspend an instance, Compute Engine discards the data of any Local SSD disks attached to the instance by default.' Shutting down from inside the guest OS also discards it, as does Spot preemption and a max-run-duration STOP. The only exception is a Preview feature (gcloud beta ... stop --discard-local-ssd=false, or REST; not from the console; at most 48 disks) that is NOT available for Titanium SSD machine types (C4, C4A, C4D, H4D, Z3 '-lssd'); preserved data is billed as storage and uses Persistent disk standard quota. Local SSD cannot be snapshotted; copy anything you want to keep to a Hyperdisk/Persistent Disk or a bucket before stopping. Not stated by Google: whether discarded Local SSD capacity keeps billing while the VM sits stopped. The wording is 'billed for the total capacity of the disk for the lifetime of the instance that it is attached to' and 'You can't delete Local SSD disks unless you delete the instance', so treat deletion of the VM as the only certain way to end Local SSD charges. Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/disks/local-ssd

Egress for a few hundred MB of logs: inbound transfer is free. Premium Tier (the default) internet egress from us-central1: first 1 GiB per month per account free, then $0.12 per GiB (1 GiB to 1 TiB tier) to North America, Europe or most of Asia; $0.15 to Middle East/Africa; $0.19 to Australia, Indonesia, Korea, South America; $0.23 to China. So 300 to 500 MB is $0.00 if it falls in the free first GiB and at most about $0.04 to $0.06 otherwise (0.5 GiB x $0.12). Standard Tier: first 200 GiB per month free, then $0.085 per GiB. Copying to a Cloud Storage bucket in the same region has no network charge ('Data moves within the same location'); normal bucket storage charges apply. An in-use external IPv4 address costs $0.005/hr ($0.12/day) on a standard VM, $0.0025/hr on Spot. Sources: https://cloud.google.com/vpc/network-pricing , https://cloud.google.com/storage/pricing

Spot: 'If Compute Engine preempts Spot VMs less than one minute after they are created, you are not billed'; Spot prices can change up to once a day; Local SSD on Spot is billed at the lower Spot local SSD rate; preemption loses Local SSD data. Sources: https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/spot , https://cloud.google.com/spot-vms/pricing

Free tier: irrelevant at this scale. Always-free Compute Engine is one e2-micro per month in us-west1, us-central1 or us-east1, 30 GB-months of standard persistent disk and 1 GB of outbound transfer from North America per month. The Free Trial is a $300 credit valid for 90 days; while the billing account is still a Free Trial account you cannot request a quota increase or add GPUs. Standard persistent disk pricing also shows the first 30 GiB-month free. Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/free/docs/free-cloud-features

Quotas that gate storage (per region; values differ per project and are not published, so they must be read on the project's Quotas page): 'Local SSD per machine family (GB)', 'Hyperdisk Balanced Capacity (GB)', 'Hyperdisk Balanced IOPS', 'Hyperdisk Balanced Throughput (MB/s)', 'Persistent disk SSD (GB)' (covers pd-ssd and pd-balanced). Hyperdisk baseline IOPS/throughput do not count against quota. Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/resource-usage
storage.budget_alerts:
All from Google pages read on 2026-11-20 (first party).

How to create one: Google Cloud console > Billing > Budgets & alerts > Create budget. (1) In Define choose 'Alerts only' and name it. (2) Scope: time range (monthly default, quarterly, yearly or custom), plus optional filters by project, service (for example Compute Engine) and, for billing-account budgets, labels. (3) Amount: a specified amount or last period's spend. (4) Threshold rules: defaults are 50%, 90% and 100% of the budget; each rule triggers on Actual or Forecasted spend (custom-range budgets cannot use Forecasted). (5) Notifications, then Finish. Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/budgets

Who can create one: on the Cloud Billing account, a role with billing.budgets.create (plus get/list and billing.accounts.getSpendingInformation), i.e. Billing Account Administrator or Billing Account Costs Manager. Without billing-account access, a project user with billing.resourcebudgets.read / billing.resourcebudgets.write on a project can create a single-project budget. Pub/Sub notifications additionally need Pub/Sub Admin on the topic's project.

What notifications do: email to Billing Account Administrators and Billing Account Users by default; optionally to Project Owners (single-project budgets only); optionally to arbitrary addresses through Cloud Monitoring email notification channels; optionally a Pub/Sub topic, which receives budget status messages multiple times per day and can drive automation.

What a budget does NOT do (verified): 'Setting an alerts-only budget doesn't automatically cap Google Cloud or Google Maps Platform usage or spending ... they don't automatically prevent the use or billing of your services when the alerts-only budget amount or threshold rules are met or exceeded.' Alerts also lag: 'it may take several hours before receiving the first email or Pub/Sub notification' after creating a budget, and 'there is a delay between your use of Google Cloud resources, and the usage costs reporting to Cloud Billing', so Google recommends setting the budget below available funds. For a one to three day job, an alert can easily arrive after most of the money is spent.

Spend cap budgets (a newer, separate budget type) do pause usage at 100% of the budget, but they do not help here: eligible services are only Gemini API, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI), Cloud Run and Cloud Run functions, not Compute Engine, and 'Spend caps don't pause any on-going, fixed usage associated with persistent resources (such as compute and storage services), which remain active and continue to accrue charges.' Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/budgets-spend-caps

Mechanisms that actually stop spend:
1. VM run-time limit: create the VM with --max-run-duration=DURATION (or --termination-time=RFC3339) and --instance-termination-action=STOP or DELETE. Range 30 seconds to 120 days; termination may begin up to 30 seconds late; the timer resets if the VM is stopped and restarted. 'A VM's local SSD data cannot be preserved when the VM is automatically stopped due to a time limit', and with gcloud a VM that has local SSDs and action STOP must also pass --discard-local-ssds-at-termination-timestamp=true. STOP ends vCPU/memory charges but leaves disks billing; DELETE ends the VM and its local SSD (persistent disks only if set to auto-delete). Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/limit-vm-runtime
2. Shutting down from inside the guest at the end of the build script (sudo shutdown -h now): compute billing stops once the instance reaches STOPPING; this discards Local SSD data. Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/stop-start-instance
3. Instance schedules (scheduled stop): can run up to 15 minutes late, need the Compute Engine Service Agent to hold Compute Instance Admin (v1), and 'You can't use instance schedules to stop an instance that has Local SSD disks', so they do not work for any local-SSD option. Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/schedule-instance-start-stop
4. Budget Pub/Sub notification driving a Cloud Run function that stops the VMs, or that disables billing on the project. Disabling billing is drastic ('shutting down all resources. Resources might be irretrievably deleted') and, because of reporting delay, 'doesn't guarantee that you won't spend more than your budget'. Sources: https://docs.cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/control-usage , https://docs.cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/disable-billing-with-notifications
5. Quotas bound how much can be running at once (vCPUs, disk GB) but do not bound spend over time. Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/resource-usage

Practical reading for this job: use a budget with low thresholds as an early-warning only, and rely on a max-run-duration with DELETE (or STOP plus a persistent boot disk) as the hard stop; nothing at the billing-account level will stop a Compute Engine VM by itself.
caveats: Method: Google's pricing pages (cloud.google.com/compute/disks-image-pricing, /products/compute/pricing/*, /spot-vms/pricing, /vpc/network-pricing) came back truncated through the normal page-fetch tool, so I retrieved the raw HTML with plain HTTP GETs and read the embedded tables. The tables in the static HTML are the default region, Iowa (us-central1); this is corroborated by cloud.google.com/products/block-storage, which states 'All prices are for the Iowa (us-central1) region' and lists the same Hyperdisk and Persistent Disk rates. I did not open the per-SKU pages at cloud.google.com/skus or the pricing calculator, and nothing was checked against a real billing account.

Titanium SSD per-GiB on-demand rates (C4D and C4 $0.16, C4A $0.12, Z3 $0.08, H4D about $0.113 per GiB-month) and all per-vCPU / per-GiB-memory component rates are DERIVED by me from Google's whole-machine price tables (differences between machine types), not quoted lines. They reproduce the published machine prices to six decimals, and the same subtraction on the Spot page reproduces Google's explicitly published C4D Spot local SSD rate, but treat them as derived.

Discrepancy on Google's own pages: the block-storage marketing page lists Local SSD at $0.036 per GB for us-central1, whereas the disk pricing page lists $0.000109589 per GiB-hour ($0.08 per GiB-month) on demand; $0.036 equals the 3-year resource-CUD column. I used the on-demand $0.08 figure.

Daily costs are hourly rate x 24; monthly equivalents use Google's 730-hour month. '2 TB' was costed as 2,048 GiB (2 TiB) for network disks. Local SSD comes only in fixed steps, so the practical sizes are 2,250 GiB (C4D/C4A 64- and 32-vCPU lssd shapes) or 3,000 GiB (8 x 375 on N2/N2D, c4d-96, c4-48, any Z3); 1,875 GiB (c4-*-32-lssd) is only 2.01 TB decimal before filesystem overhead.

Bundled '-lssd' storage is tied to machine size: on C4D you cannot get 2 TB of Titanium SSD below 64 vCPUs, so the storage choice partly dictates the VM. If a smaller or different VM is wanted, Hyperdisk Balanced is the only fast storage that sizes independently on C4/C4D/N4.

Hyperdisk Balanced bills on provisioned performance, and the defaults for a 2 TiB volume (15,288 IOPS, 2,400 MiB/s) cost $10.38/day versus $5.39/day at baseline; set IOPS and throughput explicitly. Performance can be changed only once every 4 hours. Its 140 MiB/s free baseline (about 147 MB/s) is marginally below the stated 150 MB/s peak write rate, so provision some headroom (each extra 100 MiB/s is $4/month, about $0.13/day).

Google's documentation does not say explicitly whether Local SSD capacity whose data was discarded continues to be billed while the VM remains stopped. Assume it might, and delete the VM rather than leaving it stopped.

Every VM also needs a boot disk, not included in the per-day storage figures: for example 100 GiB Hyperdisk Balanced at baseline is $0.26/day, or 100 GiB pd-balanced $0.33/day, and it keeps billing while the VM is stopped.
Spot figures are a snapshot from 2026-11-20; Google says Spot prices can change up to once per day. On-demand prices exclude tax and any negotiated discounts.

Disk quota values for the target project (Local SSD per machine family, Hyperdisk Balanced capacity/IOPS/throughput, Persistent disk SSD GB) could not be checked because no cloud account was accessed; new or free-trial projects may have limits below 2 TB or below 64 vCPUs and free-trial accounts cannot request increases.

Inference, not from a Google page: the 6 GB memory-mapped file set will be served from the Linux page cache once read, so that part of the workload depends on RAM rather than disk IOPS; the disk choice mainly matters for the 1.5 to 2 TB of output writes.
No third-party figures are used in this answer. A web search surfaced third-party aggregators (for example gcloud-compute.com), which I did not rely on.

findings.question: 1. Does CPUS_ALL_REGIONS = 32 really cap total vCPUs across all regions, blocking a 128- or 192-vCPU VM regardless of regional quotas?
findings.answer: Yes. Google's Compute Engine allocation-quotas page (console name 'CPUs (All Regions)') says: "To help protect Compute Engine systems and other users, some new accounts and projects also have a global CPUs (All Regions) quota. That quota applies to all regions and is measured as a sum of all your vCPUs in all regions." It applies in addition to regional quotas; the page's own example is a project with 48 regional vCPUs left but 32 global vCPUs left: you "can launch only 32 vCPUs in the us-central1 region, even though there is remaining quota in the region." So with a limit of 32 and no VMs running, the largest VM this project can start anywhere is 32 vCPUs. N2_CPUS 200 / M1_CPUS 640 / M3_CPUS 248 are irrelevant until the global quota is raised to at least the target VM's vCPU count. The page does not carve out Spot VMs from the global sum (it says both standard and preemptible VMs consume CPU quota), so Spot does not get round it.

findings.question: 2a. What quota governs the newer families (C4D, H4D, C3D, C4, Z4D, also N4)? Exact names.
findings.answer: There are NO per-family metrics named C4D_CPUS, H4D_CPUS, C3D_CPUS, C4_CPUS or Z4D_CPUS. Google's CPU quota table lists these families under one regional quota, CPUS_PER_VM_FAMILY, with a vm_family dimension (values C3D, C4, C4A, C4D, C4N, H3, H4D, M4, N4, N4A, N4D, X4, Z3, Z4D, Z4M ...). Console display name: 'CPUs per VM family' (filter by dimensions region + vm_family). Cloud Quotas API quota ID: CPUS-PER-VM-FAMILY-per-project-region (named on Google's Cloud Quotas terminology page). Error text on a miss is "Quota 'CPUS_PER_VM_FAMILY' exceeded. Limit: X in region R". Older families keep legacy per-family names: N2_CPUS, N2D_CPUS, C2_CPUS, C2D_CPUS, C3_CPUS, M1_CPUS, M2_CPUS, M3_CPUS, T2D_CPUS, T2A_CPUS. Only N1 and E2 draw from the generic regional CPUS quota ("E2 and N1 machine types share a CPU quota pool. Unless otherwise noted, all other machine types have unique, separate CPU quota pools"). Note C3 (not C3D) is the legacy C3_CPUS = 24 on this project.

findings.question: 2b. What is the default CPUS_PER_VM_FAMILY for a project that has never used these families, and why are they missing from the legacy regions.get quota list?
findings.answer: Default: NOT PUBLISHED. Google's pages give no numeric defaults for any CPU quota; the Cloud Quotas docs only say "Quota values are specific to your project, folder, and organization." The only evidence is community: a Sept 2025 Google Developer Forum thread reports an N4 insert failing with "Quota 'CPUS_PER_VM_FAMILY' exceeded. Limit: 0.0 in region us-west4", the quota row appearing in the console only after the failed attempt, and a respondent explaining the row was an adjustable quota pre-configured at 0 that the console had not been showing. So assume the C4D/H4D/C3D value may be 0 or small and must be read from the console/Cloud Quotas API, not assumed. Why missing from regions.get: Google does not state this explicitly. Inference: the legacy Compute API quotas[] list is a flat {metric, limit, usage} list with no dimension field, while these families are one metric split by vm_family; a March 2025 forum poster likewise could not see CPUS_PER_VM_FAMILY in `gcloud compute regions describe us-central1` or `project-info describe`. Google's Cloud Quotas known-issues page also says the console "doesn't support quota adjustment requests for quotas that have no prior usage" and that you must use the REST API or gcloud CLI instead (its example is the local-SSD-per-VM-family quota). Absence from the legacy list therefore means 'not visible there', not 'unlimited'.

findings.question: 3. What quotas apply to Hyperdisk (capacity, IOPS, throughput) and local SSD, and what are typical defaults?
findings.answer: Hyperdisk Balanced: capacity 'Hyperdisk Balanced Capacity (GB)' = HDB-TOTAL-GB (regional; shared with Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability, which consumes at 2x); 'Hyperdisk Balanced IOPS' = HDB-TOTAL-IOPS (per zone); 'Hyperdisk Balanced Throughput (MB/s)' = HDB-TOTAL-THROUGHPUT (per zone). Baseline performance does not consume IOPS/throughput quota: "Baseline IOPS and throughput don't affect the IOPS and throughput quota" (baseline = first 3,000 IOPS and 140 MiB/s per volume), so a boot disk left at baseline needs only capacity quota. Other Hyperdisk: HDX-TOTAL-GB (Extreme; also counts against SSD-TOTAL-GB), HDT-TOTAL-GB (Throughput; also counts against DISKS-TOTAL-GB), HDML-TOTAL-GB / HDML-TOTAL-THROUGHPUT. Persistent Disk: SSD-TOTAL-GB covers pd-ssd AND pd-balanced (this project: 500 GB); DISKS-TOTAL-GB covers pd-standard (4,096 GB). Local SSD: governed by 'Local SSD per VM family (GB)' = LOCAL_SSD_TOTAL_GB_PER_VM_FAMILY (metric compute.googleapis.com/local_ssd_total_storage_per_vm_family; limit names LOCAL-SSD-TOTAL-GB-PER-VM-FAMILY-per-project-region and -per-project-zone). Google states "LOCAL_SSD_TOTAL_GB quota has been deprecated", so the 'effectively unlimited' LOCAL_SSD_TOTAL_GB seen in the legacy list is NOT the governing figure. Only GPU families (A2 Ultra, A3, A4, G4 ...) are exempt; C4D/H4D/C3D -lssd shapes are not listed as exempt. Defaults: NOT PUBLISHED for any of these (the '500,000 IOPS' figure in the Hyperdisk Balanced page is only a worked example). C4D and H4D do not support Persistent Disk at all ("C4D doesn't support Persistent Disk"; H4D lists only Hyperdisk Balanced + Titanium SSD), so their boot disk needs HDB-TOTAL-GB quota, which the legacy list does not show for this project.

findings.question: 4. What quota governs Spot / preemptible VMs, and what happens when it is zero or absent?
findings.answer: One shared pool: PREEMPTIBLE_CPUS ('Preemptible CPUs'), plus 'Preemptible GPUs' and 'Preemptible Local SSDs (GB)'. Google's table shows no per-family preemptible CPU quota. If it has never been requested (this project's case: no entry), Spot falls back to standard quota: "If your project does not have preemptible quota, and you have never requested preemptible quota, these resources consume standard quota"; Spot docs: "In regions where you don't have preemptible quota, you can use standard quota to launch Spot VMs." So a Spot c4d/n2 VM here needs exactly the same standard quotas as on-demand (CPUs (All Regions) + family quota + local SSD per family). Warning: the fallback is one-way. "After you request preemptible quota in your project, the applicable resources can only consume preemptible quota and can't revert to consuming standard quotas"; "Once you request preemptible quota in a region, you are limited to using that quota for Spot VMs in that region." Recommendation: do NOT file a preemptible-quota request unless you intend all Spot use to live in that pool. Google does not document the case of preemptible quota explicitly set to 0 (page is silent). Flex-start VMs follow the same rule.

findings.question: 5a. How is an increase requested, and what determines approval?
findings.answer: Three routes. (1) Console: IAM & Admin > Quotas & System Limits, tick the quota, Edit, enter New value (or 'Apply for higher quota' with a justification and contact details), Submit request; needs Quota Administrator (roles/servicemanagement.quotaAdmin) or Owner/Editor. (2) gcloud, after `gcloud services enable cloudquotas.googleapis.com` (currently not enabled on this project): `gcloud quotas preferences create --project=P --service=compute.googleapis.com --quota-id=QUOTA_ID --dimensions=region=us-central1,vm_family=C4D --preferred-value=N --email=CONTACT --justification=TEXT` (contact email cannot be a group address); list IDs with `gcloud quotas info list --service=compute.googleapis.com --project=P`. (3) Cloud Quotas REST API (QuotaPreference). Fallbacks named by Google: Cloud Customer Care support case, or account team/TAM. For rows the console does not show because there is no prior usage, Google says to use gcloud/REST. What decides it: "Most quota adjustment requests are evaluated by automated systems. Their decision is based on criteria including the availability of resources, the length of time you've used Google Cloud, and other factors. Requests that don't meet the criteria are denied." Criteria are deliberately undisclosed. "Sometimes quota adjustment requests are escalated to human reviewers." Prepayment: "For quota adjustment requests that increase your quota value, you might be asked to pay in advance"; it is held as account credit. Partial approval/refusal: "Sometimes Google Cloud approves part of your increase request instead of approving the full increase, or denies the request entirely" (grantedValue vs preferredValue; reconciling=true while under review). No auto-approval threshold is published. Also: "Batching requests can increase the amount of time it takes" and "To reduce review time, group quota adjustment requests by product and area"; and quotas reset to defaults if the billing account is changed or billing is disrupted.

findings.question: 5b. What turnaround do Google's documents and recent user reports give for 128-384 vCPU requests?
findings.answer: Current Cloud Quotas and Compute Engine docs state NO processing time or SLA. The only Google-published figures found are older/adjacent: a Google Cloud blog (24 Sep 2021): "In the vast majority of cases, quota increase requests are evaluated and processed automatically ... a small number ... handled by human reviewers. They typically process your request within 2-3 business days"; and the support page for project-count quota: "We typically handle your quota requests within 2 business days." A Google support FAQ on cores quota (support.google.com/cloud/answer/6376374) would not load (HTTP 404 on three attempts); search snippets of it say a payment may be requested when a cores request goes well beyond typical usage and spend, the amount depending on billing history, use case and cores requested - treat as unverified. User reports (third-party, anecdotal): no dated 2025-26 report specific to 128-384 vCPU was found. Blogs claim modest CPU increases are auto-approved within minutes and larger ones take about 1-2 business days. Forum threads show the downside: automated denials with the stock reply to wait 48h or until the billing account has more history; a 2023 thread where a CPUS_ALL_REGIONS increase from 12 was refused and sales said quota was not their area; a 2021 case where the auto-approval granted a different value from the request; GitLab asked for 19,200 N2D CPUs per project and was granted 6,000 (partial). Net: an established org with paid billing history is better placed than those reports, but a first-ever jump from 32 to 192-384 global vCPUs with zero Compute usage is the profile most likely to go to manual review.

findings.question: 6. Does H4D require anything beyond quota (allow-listing, sales contact, specific zones, compact placement, Spot restrictions)?
findings.answer: No allow-list or sales approval is documented for a single on-demand H4D VM. H4D went GA on 4 Mar 2026; the machine-series page says "H4D instances are available on-demand, or with one- and three-year committed use discounts" and no access-request step appears. Spot is supported (H4D is not in the Spot exclusion list, and Google publishes an 'H4D Spot Preemptible VMs' SKU group); flex-start (Dynamic Workload Scheduler) is also supported. Constraints that do apply: (a) Zones: in us-central1 the regions/zones table shows H4D in us-central1-a, -b and -f, not -c; Cloud RDMA docs say to use us-central1-a (or europe-west4-b). (b) Whole-host VM: every H4D shape is 192 vCPUs, SMT off, so the quota ask is always 192 per VM. (c) "Live migration isn't supported for H4D instances" - VMs terminate on host maintenance (~30-day cadence, 7-day notice); -lssd shapes keep Local SSD data. (d) Storage: Hyperdisk Balanced only (capped at 15,000 IOPS / 240 MB/s per VM) plus Titanium SSD on -lssd shapes; no Persistent Disk; no machine images; no disk sharing; no GPUs; no custom types; internet egress capped at 1 Gbps. (e) Compact placement policy and a Falcon RDMA VPC (second IRDMA vNIC, MTU 8896, max-distance <= 3) are needed ONLY for multi-node Cloud RDMA clusters, not for one VM; with Spot, VMs "might not be compactly collocated". (f) The account team/sales IS required for reserved capacity: capacity blocks, and future reservations (calendar mode needs standard CPU quota, 1-256 VMs, contact the account team beyond that or if you are not eligible).

findings.question: 7. Is there any N2 / M1 / M3 machine this customer could launch after raising ONLY CPUS_ALL_REGIONS?
findings.answer: Yes - all of them fit the existing us-central1 regional quotas; only the global quota blocks them. N2_CPUS 200 covers every N2 shape up to n2-highmem-128 (128 vCPU, 864 GB), n2-standard-128, n2-highcpu-96: needs CPUs (All Regions) >= 128. M1_CPUS 640 covers m1-megamem-96 (96 vCPU, 1,433.6 GB; global >= 96), m1-ultramem-40 (961 GB), m1-ultramem-80 (1,922 GB) and m1-ultramem-160 (160 vCPU, 3,844 GB; global >= 160). M3_CPUS 248 covers m3-megamem-64 (976 GB), m3-megamem-128 (128 vCPU, 1,952 GB), m3-ultramem-32 (976 GB), m3-ultramem-64 (1,952 GB), m3-ultramem-128 (128 vCPU, 3,904 GB): global >= 128. (Not asked but also true: regional CPUS 200 covers N1/E2 up to n1-highmem-96; C2D_CPUS 100 covers c2d-*-56.) INSTANCES 24 is not a constraint for one VM. Conditions: (i) boot/data disks must fit existing disk quota - pd-balanced/pd-ssd share SSD_TOTAL_GB = 500 GB; pd-standard has 4,096 GB (N2 only; M3 does not support pd-standard); Hyperdisk Balanced on N2 requires contacting the account team per Google's Hyperdisk page. (ii) Optional Local SSD (n2-highmem-128 takes 16 or 24 x 375 GiB) is governed by the per-VM-family local SSD quota, whose value for this project is unknown. (iii) N2 above 80 vCPUs runs on Ice Lake only; M1 and M3 are 'available in only select zones' (M3 is in us-central1-a/b/c, not -f). (iv) Quota is not capacity: a zone can still return a resource-availability error. So the single-request fast path is: raise CPUs (All Regions) to 128 (or 160) and run n2-highmem-128.

findings.question: Supporting facts: shapes of the five target machines (drives the quota values).
findings.answer: From Google's machine-series pages: n2-highmem-128 = 128 vCPU, 864 GB, Local SSD optional (16 or 24 x 375 GiB). c4d-standard-192-lssd = 192 vCPU, 744 GB, 16 x 375 GiB = 6,000 GiB Titanium SSD. c4d-standard-384-lssd = 384 vCPU, 1,488 GB, 32 x 375 GiB = 12,000 GiB. h4d-highmem-192-lssd = 192 vCPU (no SMT), 1,488 GB, 10 x 375 GiB = 3,750 GiB. c3d-standard-180-lssd = 180 vCPU, 720 GB, 16 x 375 GiB = 6,000 GiB. All five families are listed in us-central1-a/b/c/f except H4D (a/b/f only). C4D and C3D support Spot; C3D supports pd-balanced/pd-ssd and Hyperdisk; C4D and H4D are Hyperdisk-only for persistent storage.

quota_requests_needed.quotas: REQUIRED: 'CPUs (All Regions)' / CPUS_ALL_REGIONS (global): 32 -> 128 minimum (ask 136-160 if any other VM must run alongside). NOT NEEDED: N2_CPUS us-central1 already 200. Disk: none if boot+data on pd-balanced/pd-ssd total <= 500 GB (SSD_TOTAL_GB) or on pd-standard <= 4,096 GB; otherwise raise 'Persistent Disk SSD (GB)' / SSD-TOTAL-GB us-central1 to the size needed. ONLY IF Local SSD is attached: 'Local SSD per VM family (GB)' / LOCAL_SSD_TOTAL_GB_PER_VM_FAMILY, region us-central1, vm_family N2: 6,000 GB (16 disks) or 9,000 GB (24 disks) - check current value first, it is not in the legacy list. Spot: nothing extra (falls back to standard quota); do not request Preemptible CPUs.
quota_requests_needed.where_to_request: Console: IAM & Admin > Quotas & System Limits, filter service 'Compute Engine API', quota 'CPUs (All Regions)', Edit > New value > Submit request. One quota, visible in the console, so no Cloud Quotas API needed.

quota_requests_needed.for_machine: c4d-standard-192-lssd (192 vCPU, 744 GB, 6,000 GiB Titanium SSD)
quota_requests_needed.quotas: 1) 'CPUs (All Regions)' / CPUS_ALL_REGIONS: 32 -> 192 minimum (suggest 200). 2) 'CPUs per VM family' / CPUS_PER_VM_FAMILY, quota ID CPUS-PER-VM-FAMILY-per-project-region, dimensions region=us-central1, vm_family=C4D: -> 192. 3) 'Local SSD per VM family (GB)' / LOCAL_SSD_TOTAL_GB_PER_VM_FAMILY, region=us-central1, vm_family=C4D: -> 6,000 GB. 4) 'Hyperdisk Balanced Capacity (GB)' / HDB-TOTAL-GB, us-central1: at least the boot disk size (e.g. 100-200 GB) - check current value; C4D cannot boot from Persistent Disk. 5) Hyperdisk Balanced IOPS / Throughput (HDB-TOTAL-IOPS, HDB-TOTAL-THROUGHPUT, per zone): only if provisioning above the free 3,000 IOPS / 140 MiB/s baseline. Spot: same quotas; none extra.

If rows are absent (no prior usage), enable cloudquotas.googleapis.com and use `gcloud quotas preferences create --service=compute.googleapis.com --quota-id=CPUS-PER-VM-FAMILY-per-project-region --dimensions=region=us-central1,vm_family=C4D --preferred-value=192 --email=... --justification=...`; confirm exact quota IDs with `gcloud quotas info list --service=compute.googleapis.com`. Submit all Compute Engine/us-central1 items together.

quota_requests_needed.for_machine: c4d-standard-384-lssd (384 vCPU, 1,488 GB, 12,000 GiB Titanium SSD)
quota_requests_needed.quotas: 1) 'CPUs (All Regions)' / CPUS_ALL_REGIONS: 32 -> 384 minimum (suggest 400). 2) 'CPUs per VM family' / CPUS_PER_VM_FAMILY (CPUS-PER-VM-FAMILY-per-project-region), region=us-central1, vm_family=C4D: -> 384. 3) 'Local SSD per VM family (GB)' / LOCAL_SSD_TOTAL_GB_PER_VM_FAMILY, region=us-central1, vm_family=C4D: -> 12,000 GB. 4) 'Hyperdisk Balanced Capacity (GB)' / HDB-TOTAL-GB us-central1: >= boot disk size. 5) Hyperdisk Balanced IOPS/Throughput (zonal) only if above baseline. quota_requests_needed.for_machine: h4d-highmem-192-lssd (192 vCPU no-SMT, 1,488 GB, 3,750 GiB Titanium SSD)
quota_requests_needed.quotas: 1) 'CPUs (All Regions)' / CPUS_ALL_REGIONS: 32 -> 192 minimum (suggest 200). 2) 'CPUs per VM family' / CPUS_PER_VM_FAMILY (CPUS-PER-VM-FAMILY-per-project-region), region=us-central1, vm_family=H4D: -> 192. 3) 'Local SSD per VM family (GB)' / LOCAL_SSD_TOTAL_GB_PER_VM_FAMILY, region=us-central1, vm_family=H4D: -> 3,750 GB. 4) 'Hyperdisk Balanced Capacity (GB)' / HDB-TOTAL-GB us-central1: >= boot disk size (H4D supports only Hyperdisk Balanced for persistent disks). No RDMA, placement-policy or reservation quota needed for a single VM. Create in us-central1-a, -b or -f (not -c).

quota_requests_needed.quotas: 1) 'CPUs (All Regions)' / CPUS_ALL_REGIONS: 32 -> 180 minimum (suggest 192-200). 2) 'CPUs per VM family' / CPUS_PER_VM_FAMILY (CPUS-PER-VM-FAMILY-per-project-region), region=us-central1, vm_family=C3D: -> 180. 3) 'Local SSD per VM family (GB)' / LOCAL_SSD_TOTAL_GB_PER_VM_FAMILY, region=us-central1, vm_family=C3D: -> 6,000 GB. 4) Disk: none if boot is pd-balanced/pd-ssd within the existing 500 GB SSD_TOTAL_GB (C3D supports Persistent Disk); HDB-TOTAL-GB only if choosing Hyperdisk Balanced. Note the existing C3_CPUS = 24 is for C3, not C3D, and does not help.

quota_requests_needed.for_machine: All targets - things NOT to request
quota_requests_needed.quotas: Do not request 'Preemptible CPUs' / PREEMPTIBLE_CPUS or 'Preemptible Local SSDs (GB)' just to use Spot: with none ever requested, Spot uses standard quota, and once requested Spot can only use the preemptible pool. 'VM instances' (INSTANCES 24) cannot and need not be requested (derived automatically from CPU quota). LOCAL_SSD_TOTAL_GB is deprecated - ignore it. Ask only for what one VM needs plus small headroom: larger asks raise the chance of manual review or partial approval.

quota.realistic_lead_time: Estimate, not a Google commitment (current Google docs publish no SLA). Fast path - n2-highmem-128, one request raising 'CPUs (All Regions)' 32 -> 128: plausibly minutes to a few hours if the automated system approves it; plan for 1-3 business days. C4D-192 / H4D-192 / C3D-180 (global quota plus per-family CPU, per-family local SSD and possibly Hyperdisk capacity, some rows not visible in the console until the Cloud Quotas API is enabled): plan for 2-5 business days, since Google's only published figure for human review is 'typically 2-3 business days' (2021 Google blog) and multiple line items slow review. C4D-384 (384 global vCPUs from 32, no Compute history): 3-10 business days, with a real chance of partial approval, a prepayment request, or an automated denial followed by a support case or account-team escalation; allow up to about 2 weeks before treating it as blocked. Add roughly 15 minutes after approval for the new limit to propagate. Approval of quota does not guarantee capacity for 192/384-vCPU shapes in a given zone. Recommended sequencing: file the 128-vCPU global request first (unblocks N2/M1/M3 on existing regional quota), and file the newer-family requests in parallel.
caveats: Default quota values for CPUS_PER_VM_FAMILY, local SSD per VM family and Hyperdisk are not published by Google; the customer's real values for C4D/H4D/C3D must be read from the console Quotas & System Limits page or `gcloud quotas info list` (requires enabling cloudquotas.googleapis.com). I had no account access and ran no cloud CLI.

The explanation for why the newer families are absent from the legacy regions.get list is an inference backed by forum reports, not an explicit Google statement. Absent does not mean unlimited; community evidence shows such quotas can be pre-set to 0.

The Cloud Quotas quota ID for 'CPUs (All Regions)' could not be confirmed on a Google page (only CPUS-per-project-region and CPUS-PER-VM-FAMILY-per-project-region were found); look it up with `gcloud quotas info list` or just use the console for that one.

support.google.com/cloud/answer/6376374 ('Request cores quota increase FAQs') returned HTTP 404 on three fetch attempts; statements attributed to it (payment may be requested depending on billing history and cores requested) come from search-result snippets only. docs.cloud.google.com/docs/quotas/quota-adjustments also returned 404; the same content was read from docs.cloud.google.com/docs/quotas/overview.

Turnaround evidence is thin: Google's '2-3 business days' is from a 2021 blog and the '2 business days' figure is for project-count quota; no dated 2025-26 user report specific to 128-384 vCPU requests was found. The lead-time range is my estimate. Third-party blogs (oneuptime, devopsaitoolkit) are cross-checks only.

Google's docs do not say explicitly that -lssd Titanium SSD on C4D/H4D/C3D consumes 'Local SSD per VM family' quota; this is inferred from the fact that only GPU families are listed as exempt. Treat the local-SSD line items as required until the console shows otherwise.

The statement that Hyperdisk Balanced on N2 requires contacting the account team, and the per-zone family availability table, were extracted by an automated page reader from Google's pages; verify in the console before relying on them. Zone-level availability of the specific 192/384-vCPU shapes was not confirmed, only the series.
Behaviour when preemptible quota exists but is explicitly 0 is not documented by Google; the documented fallback to standard quota applies only when preemptible quota has never been requested.
Changing the project's billing account, or a billing disruption, resets quotas to defaults (Google's statement) - do this before, not after, requesting increases.
Pricing was out of scope for this step (the seven questions are all quota questions); no prices or per-vCPU/per-GB rates are reported here.
The local memory directory was re-checked as the user asked; no memory file mentions Google Cloud quotas or Compute Engine, so nothing there changes these findings.
